chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Market Cycles, Era by Era

lessons.title: From the Banyan Tree to the Sensex: Indian Markets Before 1991

body.text: India had booms, busts and speculators long before it had a Sensex. What it lacked for most of the twentieth century was an economy open enough, and rules light enough, for a long bull market to take hold.

children.text: Chapter 2 followed cycles in Holland, Britain, the United States and Japan. This chapter brings the same lens home. We start with the 130 years before 1991: a cotton-fuelled mania in 1860s Bombay that could have come straight out of Lesson 2.1, a long post-independence stretch in which the state tightly controlled capital, and a 1980s awakening that created India's first mass generation of shareholders. Each era shaped the market you trade in on Zerodha today.

In the 1850s a small group of brokers in Bombay met under banyan trees near the Town Hall, in the area now known as Horniman Circle, to trade shares of banks, cotton mills and trading companies. As their numbers grew they kept being moved on, until in 1874 they settled on a street that became synonymous with Indian markets: Dalal Street, dalal meaning broker. In 1875 they formed the Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association. That body is today's BSE, the oldest stock exchange in Asia.
Bombay's First Mania: The Cotton Boom of 1861 to 1865

The displacement came from the other side of the world. When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, the Union blockade cut off cotton from the southern United States, the main supplier to the mills of Lancashire in England. British buyers turned to India. Cotton prices soared, and an enormous flow of silver and money poured into Bombay, the hub of the trade. With more cash than sensible places to put it, Bombay's merchants turned to shares. Dozens of new banks, financial associations and land reclamation companies were floated. The most famous was the Back Bay Reclamation Company, set up to reclaim land from the sea, whose shares reportedly traded at many times their issue value. The star of the era was Premchand Roychand, a broker so dominant he was known as the Cotton King.

markDefs.definition: Contracts to buy or sell shares on a fixed future settlement date at an agreed price, with little or no money paid upfront. Similar in effect to the forward contracts of Tulip Mania.

children.text: Credit did the rest. Banks, including the Bank of Bombay, lent freely against shares as collateral, and speculators traded heavily in

for future settlement. When the Civil War ended in April 1865, American cotton was expected back on the market and Indian cotton prices collapsed. Settlement fell due in mid 1865 on contracts that could no longer be honoured, share prices crashed, and firm after firm failed. The Bank of Bombay, weighed down by loans secured on worthless shares, collapsed and was liquidated in 1868.

body.caption: Bombay 1861 to 1865 through Kindleberger's five stages from Lesson 2.1

cells: 1. Displacement
The American Civil War cuts off US cotton, and Indian cotton becomes suddenly, hugely valuable
2. Boom
Cotton money floods Bombay, and banks lend against shares
3. Euphoria
New companies floated almost weekly, reclamation shares trade at many times their issue value, time bargains multiply
4. Distress
The Civil War ends in April 1865 and cotton prices fall
5. Revulsion
Settlements fail, companies collapse, and the Bank of Bombay is liquidated in 1868

body.text: The mania left a physical legacy you can still see in Mumbai. Before the crash, Premchand Roychand donated money for the University of Bombay's library and clock tower, and the Rajabai Tower, named after his mother, still stands next to the Bombay High Court. And the reclaimed land schemes of that era were early steps in the long process that eventually created much of today's south Mumbai waterfront.

body.title: Connect the Pattern
body.question: Which feature of the Bombay mania of the 1860s is most similar to the South Sea Bubble of 1720 from Lesson 2.1?
options: Both were caused by a new railway technology
In both, lenders provided credit against the very shares being bought, so falling prices destroyed both investors and lenders
Both were ended by a government guarantee of share prices
Both involved trading in tulip bulbs
body.explanation: The Bank of Bombay lent against shares just as the South Sea Company lent against its own stock. Rising prices created more collateral and more lending. When prices fell, the loans went bad at the same time as the investments, which is why a bank collapsed alongside the speculators.

events.title: The exchange is formed
events.description: The Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association is founded in Bombay, the forerunner of BSE.

events.title: More exchanges
events.description: Brokers organise in Ahmedabad in 1894, serving its textile mills, and the Calcutta Stock Exchange is formed in 1908, serving jute, tea and coal companies.

events.title: Swadeshi capital
events.description: The Swadeshi movement encourages Indians to back Indian enterprises. In 1907 the Tata Iron and Steel Company raises about ₹2.3 crore from thousands of Indian investors within weeks, a landmark for domestic capital.

events.title: The Depression reaches India
events.description: Collapsing crop prices hit farm incomes and trade, as covered in Lesson 2.2. Industrial shares are weak for much of the decade.

events.title: Independence and capital controls
events.description: The Capital Issues (Control) Act gives the government power to approve every share issue, including its timing and price.

events.title: The legal framework
events.description: The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act and the Companies Act are passed, and life insurance is nationalised to form LIC. BSE becomes the first exchange recognised under the new law in 1957.

events.title: Unit Trust of India
events.description: The government sets up UTI, and its US-64 scheme becomes the first mass-market vehicle for Indian households to own a slice of the stock market.

children.text: Independent India chose a planned economy, with the state leading heavy industry and private business operating under licences, quotas and price controls. The goals were self-reliance and fairness. The side effect was a stock market that could not really cycle in the way Western markets did. Large parts of the economy were off limits to listed companies, the government decided when and at what price companies could raise money, and tax rates made holding financial wealth deeply unattractive. Economic growth averaged only around 3.5% a year for three decades, and equity markets stayed small and dominated by a few business houses.

body.caption: The controls that shaped Indian markets before 1991

cells: Controller of Capital Issues (from 1947)
Companies needed approval to issue shares, and the price was set by formula, usually well below what the market would pay. Issues were often underpriced
Industrial licensing
Companies needed government permission to expand capacity, which capped growth for even the best-run businesses
Nationalisation
Life insurance in 1956, 14 major banks in 1969 and 6 more in 1980 moved large sectors out of private and listed ownership
MRTP Act (1969)
Large business groups faced extra approvals to grow, limiting their expansion
Very high taxes
The top marginal income tax rate, including surcharge, reached 97.75% in 1973-74, and wealth tax applied on top. Holding large amounts of shares openly was punishing
FERA (1973)
Most foreign-controlled companies had to cut foreign ownership to 40%, selling shares to Indians at controlled prices, as covered in Lesson 2.3

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Including surcharge, India's top marginal income tax rate in 1973-74 was ___%.
body.explanation: A base rate of 85% plus a 15% surcharge on that tax gave 85% × 1.15 = 97.75%. On the highest slab, a taxpayer kept just ₹2.25 of every extra ₹100 earned. Rates like these pushed wealth into gold, real estate and undeclared cash rather than listed shares.

children.text: Three forces changed the picture. First, the FERA share sales of the 1970s had given many middle-class families their first shares, often at bargain prices, and a taste for more. Second, Dhirubhai Ambani's Reliance Textile Industries went public in 1977 and deliberately courted small investors, using convertible debentures and heavy retail participation to build one of the largest shareholder bases in the country. Third, the government began to relax. The 1985 Budget cut the top personal income tax rate to 50% and loosened some licensing, and markets responded strongly. The BSE launched the Sensex in 1986, with a base value of 100 in 1978-79, and in 1988 the government created the Securities and Exchange Board of India, initially without statutory powers.

body.text: A cycle story from 1982: a group of brokers, widely reported to be based in Calcutta, sold Reliance shares short in large quantities, expecting the price to fall. Investors friendly to Reliance kept buying and demanded delivery of the shares. The short sellers could not deliver, the price rose instead of falling, and the Bombay exchange suspended trading for three days while the dispute was settled. It showed how thin, lightly regulated markets could be squeezed, and it cemented Reliance's reputation with retail shareholders.

children.text: The result showed up in the index. The Sensex rose from its base of 100 to cross 1,000 for the first time in July 1990, roughly ten times in about 11 years. That was a real bull market, even allowing for Indian inflation that averaged high single digits through the 1980s. The standard way to compare growth over different periods is the compound annual growth rate.

body.caption: Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly rate that turns the starting value into the ending value

body.title: The Sensex's First Decade
body.prompt: Treat the Sensex as rising from 100 to 1,000 over exactly 11 years. What was its CAGR, before dividends? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: CAGR = (1,000 ÷ 100) to the power 1/11, minus 1 = 10 to the power 0.0909, minus 1 ≈ 1.233 − 1 = 23.3% a year. With Indian inflation running at roughly 8% to 9% a year over the decade, the real return was still well into double digits. Compare that with the 16% long-run figure from Lesson 1.1: the Sensex's early years were among its strongest.

body.title: How you traded then vs now

columns.label: Dalal Street in the 1980s
points: Brokers shouting bids in a trading ring, known as open outcry
Physical share certificates, with transfers that could take months and frequent bad deliveries or forgeries
Trades settled in fortnightly account periods, and positions could be carried forward using badla financing
Prices known mostly to insiders, with no real-time public data

columns.label: Your Zerodha account today
points: Fully electronic order matching on NSE and BSE
Shares held in dematerialised form with NSDL or CDSL
T+1 settlement for equities, fully in place since January 2023
Live prices, order books and company filings available to everyone
SEBI as a statutory regulator with enforcement powers

children.text: The 1980s growth came with a cost. The government ran large fiscal deficits and borrowed heavily abroad, much of it short term. When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, oil prices spiked, remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf dried up, and political instability at home made foreign lenders nervous. By mid 1991 India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to roughly $1 billion, enough for only a few weeks of imports, and the government had to pledge gold abroad to raise emergency funds. It was a textbook Juglar-style credit squeeze at the scale of a whole country, and it forced the reforms that opened the next chapter of India's market history.

body.title: A Letter From 1865
body.scenario: Your great-great-grandfather was a Bombay cotton merchant. A family letter from 1864 says he borrowed from the Bank of Bombay, pledging his existing shares, to buy more shares in a land reclamation company, because "prices have only gone up for three years and cotton money will never stop." Today your cousin in Ahmedabad has pledged his mutual fund units for a loan against securities to buy more shares in a sector that has tripled in three years.
body.prompt: What went wrong for your ancestor, and what parallels should your cousin think about?
body.modelAnswer: Your ancestor made three linked mistakes. He assumed an external windfall, cotton prices inflated by a foreign war, was permanent, when it depended entirely on events he could not control. He borrowed against shares to buy more shares, so a fall in prices would shrink his collateral and his holdings at the same time. And he extrapolated three good years into the future, which is straight-line thinking from Lesson 1.1. When the war ended, cotton prices fell, settlements failed and the lender itself collapsed. Your cousin's situation has real parallels. A loan against securities uses the same loop: if the market falls, the pledged units are worth less, the lender can demand more margin or sell them, and the shares he bought with the loan are falling too. A sector that has tripled in three years may be driven by conditions that can reverse. Modern safeguards are much better: SEBI rules, regulated lenders and electronic settlement mean no repeat of 1865's chaos. But the market risk and the leverage risk are exactly the same as they were for your ancestor. The cycle-aware question is what happens to him if that sector falls 40% while the loan is outstanding.

cards.term: Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association
cards.definition: Formed in Bombay in 1875. The forerunner of BSE, the oldest stock exchange in Asia.
A speculative boom from 1861 to 1865 fuelled by soaring cotton prices during the American Civil War. It collapsed when the war ended, bringing down the Bank of Bombay.
The authority that, from 1947 until 1992, approved share issues and set their prices by formula.
The flagship scheme of the Unit Trust of India, launched in 1964, which gave millions of Indian households indirect exposure to shares.
A traditional carry-forward system on Indian exchanges that let traders postpone settlement by paying or receiving a financing charge, allowing leveraged speculation.
Compound annual growth rate: (ending value ÷ starting value) to the power 1/years, minus 1.

children.text: Lesson 3.2 picks up in July 1991, with reserves nearly exhausted, and follows what happened next: liberalisation, a spectacular boom, the securities scam of 1992, the creation of NSE, and a full boom-and-bust cycle compressed into a single decade.

body.text: Historical figures in this lesson, particularly for the nineteenth century, are approximate and based on accounts that sometimes differ. The content is for education only and is not investment advice. Loans against securities and other forms of leverage carry significant risk; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser before using them.

points: Bombay's brokers traded under banyan trees in the 1850s, moved to Dalal Street in 1874, and formed the association that became BSE in 1875
The 1861 to 1865 cotton boom produced a full Kindleberger-style mania, with lending against shares and time bargains, ending in the collapse of the Bank of Bombay
After 1947, capital issue controls, licensing, nationalisation and top tax rates as high as 97.75% held Indian equity markets back for decades
FERA share sales, Reliance's retail-focused IPO in 1977, and tax cuts in 1985 created India's first mass generation of shareholders
The Sensex rose from 100 in 1978-79 to 1,000 in July 1990, a CAGR above 20% a year before dividends
Heavy borrowing and the 1990 oil shock led to the 1991 balance of payments crisis, a nationwide credit squeeze that forced sweeping reforms
